title: Espousing proper movement patterns for perfect dynamic postures
summary: NH explains dynamic posture: applying the movement patterns learned in the gym (hinge, squat, pulling with the back) to everyday life, where most injuries actually happen. He covers walking, pulling, lifting from the floor, squatting, biceps and shoulder injuries, and warns that lifting strength does not transfer to sport-specific skills.
claims: Static and dynamic posture feed into each other; how you hold your body at rest influences how you move, so both must be worked on
Most injuries are domestic accidents, not gym injuries: lifting a box, starting a lawn mower and tearing a biceps, slipping on ice
Gym movement patterns replicate natural human movements; the squat was not invented, resistance was simply added to knee flexion
Most of the 'functional training' discourse is stupid: every movement that reinforces a good pattern and strengthens muscles carries over to daily life
In total tonnage and activity you do far more outside the gym than inside it, so daily movement quality matters a lot
In the gym you're warmed up and mentally primed, so people rarely get hurt on heavy lifts; they get hurt doing something trivial
When picking something up from the floor, hip hinge or squat down to it; never round your back, people blow their back out picking up a sock
Good movement patterns load muscles while poor ones load joints; people hang on their joints because it feels more comfortable
Walk upright with head up and no forward head posture; let arms and shoulders swing naturally
When walking, push off the floor rather than stamping; pushing involves glutes and hamstrings, stamping overloads quads and knee tendons
Pull with the back, not the arms: engage the scapula and use the arms as ropes; arm-only pulling injures biceps, elbows and shoulders
Learning to open doors with the lats rather than the arms is easier and safer
Resting completely for lower back pain makes it worse because the muscles protecting the spine atrophy
Westerners have lost the deep squat pattern; asked to squat fully, about 95% would tip over or have huge butt wink, while squatting cultures practise it daily
Without a squat pattern people are forced into pure hip hinges for heavy objects and get hurt
Low-intensity daily tonnage with poor patterns feeds tendinitis and tendon pain that worsens minor gym damage, creating a vicious circle
If it's effective for picking up 400 lb, it's effective for picking up a box
Squat, deadlift and bench are functional training; bench reinforces tucking the shoulders back instead of overusing the rotator cuff
Many everyday shoulder injuries come from weak rear delts and back muscles letting the shoulder overextend
Lifting doesn't make you a superhero: strength doesn't transfer automatically to a sport movement; many lifters tear a rotator cuff throwing a baseball
exercises: push glutes back, neutral spine, let hamstrings stretch
teaches safe lifting from the floor
full depth, no butt wink; practise it
lost pattern that protects the lower back when lifting objects
